If it didn't run in my extended family, I would have spent countless years wondering what was wrong with me. Medical professionals (including one who was previously a close trusted friend) attempted to gaslight me and said that I was hysterical and that it was "all in my head". I was even fired from a job while I was in the hospital dealing with major depression from having all of these health issues. I was also very fortunate to find local EDS support groups early on, both online and in-person.

I have been in physical therapy now on and off for ten years. I will probably always be in some sort of PT for the rest of my life and I'm okay with that because I have seen the difference it has made for me. I now go every two weeks and we are working on a plan to get me back into running, one year after discharge from post-surgery ankle/foot PT! This is HUGE!

A challenge for me still is that I don't get any warning in the moment but will get post-exertional malaise, so I am constantly guessing how long I can go without getting tired.

comments.name: N.G. Krishnan
comments.body:
Every transformative leap in human history was met with a chorus of doom. 

Gutenberg’s printing press was feared; the Industrial Revolution was decried as societal ruin. Had we capitulated to the naysayers at every historical crossroads, human civilization would have stagnated centuries ago.

Banning artificial intelligence out of fear is the ultimate exercise in cutting off our nose to spite our face.

Practically every invention in human history has been a double-edged sword. Fire warms us, but it burns; electricity powers cities, but it can kill. We did not ban fire or abandon physics—we built hearths, insulated wires, and created safety standards.

The need of the hour is not panic or retreat, but smart, pragmatic guardrails against misuse. Heavy-handed restriction will not eliminate risk; it will only rob us of solutions to our greatest challenges, from accelerating life-saving medicine to solving climate crises. 

Properly guided, AI will not diminish us—it will shepherd humanity toward a non-zero-sum destiny of unprecedented progress and shared abundance.

Some people may suffer from severe complications, such as pneumonia (infection of the lungs) and encephalitis (swelling of the brain). They may need to be hospitalized and could die.

Hospitalization. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized.

Pneumonia. As many as 1 out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children.

Encephalitis. About 1 child out of every 1,000 who get measles will develop encephalitis (swelling of the brain). This can lead to convulsions and leave the child deaf or with intellectual disability.

Death. Nearly 1 to 3 of every 1,000 children who become infected with measles will die from respiratory and neurologic complications.

Complications during pregnancy. If you are pregnant and have not had the MMR vaccine, measles may cause you to give birth prematurely or have a low-birth-weight baby.

Long-term complications

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a very rare, but fatal disease of the central nervous system. It results from a measles virus infection acquired earlier in life.

charging is a big problem. we have given up on renting EVs
1) is there a convenient charger? We found some to be gone or out of order. If it a single charger site then you get to wait if someone else is charging. there are apps identifying locations but each app shows a fraction of the chargers. 
2) how long does it take to charge? The answer is often many hours. Unlikely to have one available near your hotel. A small fraction of the public chargers are fast chargers.

comments.name: Austro Girl
comments.body:
We've leased EVs long-term a couple of times/year in the alpine region. We LOVE them! They lose zero power when driving uphill on those windy, vertiginous roads, and they cost next to nothing to operate.  Yes, The learning curve at the beginning was steep -- I had the 'dude' sit in the front seat w me and walk me through the 1st one. (Hertz gave us a shell toggle, which made charging easy).  Now we just take a few minutes at the beginning, set the computer to English, and off we go. So far, the Polestar (sixt) is our favorite...(even better than the Mercedes we were once upgraded to!)

The Fiat 600 we had this fall had a 450km range, and was the lease expensive car in the fleet.  By far. We find that ski areas have chargers close to first lifts; many hotels have chargers on site; nearly every town and all rest areas have chargers. Download an app for a charger map, and you're good to go.  And... most alpine electricity is Hydro powered... and costs exponentially less than gas.  If the US had the same infrastructure, we'd buy one for over here in a heartbeat!

If you try to do it yourself, you'll constantly find yourself forty or fifty miles short of the charger you were planning to reach, and starting to panic. It adds a lot of stress to what was supposed to be a fun experience. Ask me how I know, in southern Colorado where DC fast-charging stations are far apart.

Most tout the environmental and fuel savings, which we appreciate.  But, my wife and I grew up when V8s were standard and gas was 29.9. The ev has that fast, smooth, quiet performance minus the oil changes. If only they'd revive the  bench seat.  Boomers know what I mean

It was my first time ever driving an electric car, and it was a lot of fun to speed around the fjords of Western Norway. The acceleration was so quick and fast! A week after I returned the car, Hertz emailed me to let me know I should expect to receive expect a speeding ticket from the Norwegian authorities in the mail...

Regarding charging, I was told to return the car with at least 80% charge. I didn't do this and was billed for it (it wasn't much). The car came with some kind of adapter in the trunk.

comments.name: A
comments.body: Our first experience with an EV was a Turo Tesla rental eight years ago. We didn't care for Tesla features, but enjoyed the acceleration and quiet ride of the EV. We also liked knowing that we were contributing less to air pollution. When electric car share came to downtown LA, we signed up for the service, and enjoyed zipping around greater LA in Chevy Bolts. The driving experience was more like the ICE cars we were used to, but it still had peppy acceleration and a quiet ride. When we finally decided to buy a car of our own, we bought a Bolt EUV, and we love it . The range is less than other EVs, but adequate for our needs. We live in an apartment, but I can charge for free twice a week at work, so our fuel costs are practically nil. We do pay to charge on long trips, like a recent road trip up the coast to Cambria. Stopping to charge takes longer than refiling a gas tank, but we factored it in to our travel plan, and found charger locations at restaurants and shopping centers where we could occupy the 40-60 minute wait with other activities. Another plus: owning an EV is so much cheaper because there's no oil changes and little regular required maintenance. Since that first rental almost ten years ago, we've come to appreciate EVs and do not plan to ever buy an ICE car again.

Thanks for the lively review. I look forward to reading this book.

I think Delon was a very interesting actor in part because he combined his beauty with a sense of the loner. He didn't preen and instead held the audience at bay.

His own biography informs this quality. Delon's parents divorced when he was four years old, which was very unusual in France at the time. Both parents remarried and welcomed additional children and Delon didn't fit in with these reconfigurations--to the point that he was taken in by a foster family. His foster parents died when Delon was 11 and his birth parents then sent him to boarding school. He felt rejected and acted out with wild adventures and petty criminality from a very young age. 

I was aware of rumors regarding Delon's association with the French underworld and rumors regarding Markovic. The film industry all over the world has unsavory ties and shady characters and he's not the only famous actor to be implicated in such a way. No, I'm not excusing any of Delon's actions or behaviors, just stating a fact. This book could be the beginning of a series!

Delon was indeed beautiful but he was a quietly vicious and often ruthless operator in his private life. There's an entirely separate book waiting to be written on his romantic escapades (the man was a consummate gaslighter) and connections to other underworld figures while being feted as a national treasure. Example: he was said to have been the father of the infant born to German chanteuse Nico aka Christa Paeffgen. He disputed the paternity claim, but then Delon's mother informally adopted the child, who unsurprisingly had a difficult life before his death at age 60 in 2023 from a drug overdose. His own mother! They are all cognizant of the recent science on drinking. My son and oldest just decided that last hangover was not worth it and stopped entirely. comments.name: cljuniper
comments.body: Somebody once guess-timated that the "internet" was 70% disinformation.  How did that happen?  A combo of writing style, IMHO, with writers in media including NYT using adjectives to discuss a statistical change...instead of the actual statistics.  Yes, we are visual/emotive creatures who like stories over numbers, but we have to realize that adjectives are pretty subjective, so to speak.  So, for example, what does a polling decline of a personal habit mean if the new number is 24% instead of 30%?  Yes, it's a 20% decline, but what's the range of error of the polling system?  My guess is that a 20% decline isn't anything important unless several polls over time verify the trend.  In addition, our culture has veered towards extremes being sought - in athletics, experiences, etc.  So behaviors don't seem "out of control" compared to extremes - but we should be comparing to prudent behaviors, not extremes.  So I'm sad/alarmed when people are limited to just a few drinks over a weekend due to their cost - which says to me an out of control drinking norm.  People like to make extreme statements - they get attention - but responsible media have a duty to not plunge down that path, and responsible adults have a duty to ignore extremes and seek true math understanding of what's happening, howsoever boring that seems.

There are moments of cringe, and moments where the audience may feel sympathy as as well as as ire. Are we being manipulated by the documentarian? Yes. Are we being manipulated by the subjects of the documentary? More than likely. Are we confused, as the audience, because Elizabeth Holmes may be a criminal grifter, but she also loves her children? Probably. Are we confronted with a history for her that includes men who enjoy controlling her? It does seem so. Is the documentary about Elizabeth, her husband, Nathan, or Amanda, or is it about the uncomfortable truth that no matter what we are presented in the media, things might be more complex? We Americans have gotten very very used to zero-sum thinking these past few years. We enjoy cleaving to a narrative that makes us feel better about ourselves. The sleight-of-hand” you can see everything“ is that, while entertained, we still find ourselves, confused, and perhaps even unable to admit that there is a simple “truth“ to this whole thing. Rather than decry this, we should thank the filmmakers for exposing this flaw in our reasoning to the audience.

comments.name: Phipps
comments.body:
Having spent much of my life as a chef and having lived in Scandinavia, I immediately recognize what interests me about Ursa. The best of New Nordic cooking wasn't really about tweezers, moss or expensive tasting menus. It was about looking seriously at one's own landscape and asking what cuisine could emerge from it.

Aaron Lopez appears to be doing something comparable with the Sonoran Desert: taking ingredients, traditions and knowledge specific to his region and treating them as worthy of serious cooking.

The sneering about “twigs” and “weird ingredients” misses the point. A cactus fruit isn't more pretentious than a strawberry; it's simply less familiar to most Americans. Unfamiliarity is not fraud.

I spent years cooking professionally and adore simple food. But simplicity is an aesthetic choice, not a moral virtue. I don't want every restaurant to cook like Ursa. I don't want every restaurant to cook like a trattoria either. Sometimes the pleasure of eating is encountering something you don't already understand.

comments.name: Tom L.
comments.body: Ursa is a fantastic restaurant. Brilliant is the right word. The two meals I've had there were among the most delicious and interesting I've ever had.  Here's a thought: maybe the pushback in the comments would be less and less knee-jerk if the review had been more down-to-earth and more explanatory. There's a lot of gush and a lot of unexplained words and not much straightforward. By the way it's written, the review reinforces a sense of elitism. That's the sales pitch in the review. Ursa, though, is the opposite. It's all about the earth, the plants we take for granted and ignore, the goat, an underappreciated meat. The meals are costly. I don't say they aren't. The food is subtle and bold and surprising and, in many ways, simple, like the best refined cooking always is. The prose in the review is the opposite. Maybe that's not quite the best fit for this truly special place.

There are restaurants designed for only the the highest budgets of them all. (Ursa, by the way, isn't in that category.) This is life. The comment section of a restaurant review is probably not the best place to argue about economic fairness and equity, especially since no one HAS to eat at Ursa or they won't survive. Blind populism on the left is no better than blind populism on the right. The commenters who rail against Ursa's prices are being unfair. Ursa's prices, on the other hand, are not unfair to commenters. It this was a review of a gas company, or an electricity provider, or a water supplier it would be different. It's a review of a restaurant. Everyone of us has bought what would be a luxury for others. Without exception. The world is better for the ambition and inventiveness of Mr. Lopez, not worse. That's a fact.

Be smart and only buy organic cranberries. Why? Cranberries are often contaminated by multiple pesticides used on them. Here's a list from Google AI overview: 
"Pesticides used on cranberry bogs include a mix of herbicides, insecticides, miticides, and fungicides applied primarily through water sprinkler irrigation systems (chemigation), ground rigs, or aerial spraying.

Types of Pesticides & Common Examples

• Herbicides (Weed Control): Used to manage pre- and post-emergent weeds along bogs, dikes, and ditches. Examples include:
	• Dichlobenil (Casoron)
	• Napropamide (Devrinol)
	• Norflurazon (Evital)
	• Glyphosate (Roundup)
	• Mesotrione (Callisto)
	• Sethoxydim (Poast), Clethodim (Select Max), and Clopyralid (Stinger)
• Insecticides (Insect Pests): Used to target root-to-fruit insect pests like fireworms, fruitworms, and tipworms. Commonly referenced or monitored active/legacy compounds include:
	• Chlorantraniliprole
	• Chlorpyrifos, diazinon, and azinphos-methyl (historically and regionally predominant)
	• Carbyl and legacy organophosphates like parathion/Guthion
• Fungicides & Miticides: Applied to combat fruit and vine rots/pathogenic fungi thriving in the moist bog environment, alongside biological controls (such as Bt, beneficial nematodes, or cultural Integrated Pest Management [IPM] practices)."

Eventually, I began consuming two cranberry gummies daily along with a daily bowl of oatmeal loaded with at least an eighth of a cup of dried cranberries and a three finger and thumb large pinch of pecans. For good measure, I also consume a palm full of cranberries while the oatmeal combo cooks. 

I haven't had a UTI since the beginning of June. Knock on wood.

In my 60s it was insulting to have male doctors telling me I needed to wipe front to back. A male gynecologist with a clue put me on an estrogen cream suppository. I didn't like suppositories years ago. I don't like them now. That didn't last long.

I'll stick with my current regimen.

comments.name: Marc
comments.body:
Hip-hop may be an excellent doorway into learning. But a doorway is not the destination. The destination should be mastery of writing, mathematics, science, technology, history, and independent thinking.

Richard Feynman spoke of "the pleasure of finding things out." If a hip-hop-centered curriculum helps students reconnect with school, that is a genuine achievement. But engagement and education are not the same thing. In an AI-driven world, students will need strong foundations in critical thinking, quantitative reasoning, communication, and lifelong learning.

The ultimate measure of a school is not whether students enjoy today's lessons. It is whether graduates leave with the knowledge, discipline, and habits of inquiry needed to adapt, solve problems, and keep learning throughout their lives. The question is not only whether students enjoy what they are learning, but whether they are acquiring the capabilities that will allow them to thrive in a world very different from the one they see today.

Excitement is valuable, but capability is indispensable. A good education should not simply meet students where they are. It should equip them to go where they have not yet imagined.

"The pleasure of finding things out" is a wonderful beginning. The challenge of education is ensuring that students leave with the ability to keep discovering, questioning, and learning for the rest of their lives.

The state constitution also has, since 1970, an express "Equal Rights Regardless of Sex" clause, removing any impairments based on sex.

And it has a sex neutral "Equal Parental Responsibility Clause" (in all aspects of a child's needs) since about 1990.

What is obstructing this framing is the view that there is an extraconstitutional "Divine Right of Man" (like the "Divine Right of Kings" but claimed by individual men to allow them to enforce imagined laws and legal fictions, publicly or privately, against non-men).  This is based in the Dec of Independence language "All men ... endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights . . . .".  

When George Mason from VA tried to put this "Divine Right of Man" language in the US Constitution 1787-1791 he was resoundingly rejected.  Instead only the terms Person and/or Citizen are used.

You do NOT have only a  33% of winning if you stick to your original decision.

Marilyn vos Savant dealt with this problem in a 1990 Parade magazine article.  This from Wikipedia:

“Many readers of Savant's column refused to believe switching is beneficial and rejected her explanation. After the problem appeared in Parade, approximately 10,000 readers, including nearly 1,000 with PhDs, wrote to the magazine, most of them calling Savant wrong. Even when given explanations, simulations, and formal mathematical proofs, many people still did not accept that switching is the best strategy.”

comments.name: Rich Pattis
comments.body: My favorite explanation. The problem becomes a bit simpler if you expand the number of doors to 100 (heck try 1 million). Now you choose one, and the host exposes 98 doors not known to have a car behind them. Do you stay or switch? You had a 1 in 100 chance of choosing the right door, so didn't likely choose correctly; if you didn't choose correctly, the host carefully avoids showing you where the car is by choosing which 98 doors to expose. The one unexposed door likely (99 times out of 100) has the car.

comments.name: Stewart
comments.body:
"The host hasn’t randomly eliminated a door; he has deliberately revealed a goat, using his knowledge of where the car is. Your original door still has a one-in-three chance of hiding the car, while switching gives you a two-in-three chance of winning."

This is the key point, which many explanations of the Monty Hall problem omit, or fail to state clearly. The host's knowlege changes the odds. Thank you for stating it so succinctly.

This is depressing. Apparently, Advent has now become just another casualty of commercial opportunism and widespread religious illiteracy.

For those unfamiliar with the Christian calendar—and judging by this article, there are quite a few—Advent is a season of preparation and anticipation for the coming of the Holy Child. Christmas Eve marks the eve of his birth. Christmas Day, December 25, begins the season of CHRISTMAS, which lasts—wait for it—TWELVE WHOLE DAYS! Yes, December 25 is the FIRST day of Christmas, and January 5 is the TWELFTH. Imagine that!

But leave it to predatory commercialism to take a beautiful, contemplative season like Advent, strip it of its meaning, and turn it into yet another opportunity to fleece the public. And why bother with even a passing acquaintance with the Christian calendar when religious ignorance is so wonderfully profitable? By all means, let's market a “Twelve Days of Christmas” countdown beginning December 13. Why let 1,700 years of Christian liturgical tradition interfere with a perfectly good sales opportunity?

comments.body: My first visit to Vietnam was in 1992, the first year it was open to tourism. I was fortunate to have traveled the country as a rare tourist, experiencing an unspoiled culture and pristine beaches. Nha Trang coast was empty then. We were the only people on that now-transformed beach. I went back in early 2016 to work in higher education in DaNang for 4 years. The streets in An Thoung neighborhood were dark then and a Western-style restaurant was rare. By my last year, the area had transformed, but not for the better. The digital bro-mads and party kids that are always attracted to the beach, a particularly uninteresting demographic, transformed the country. Culture clashes and criminality are now common. Prices of course, have risen, housing in particular. Things that the residents typically have to endure in the name of progress have turned DaNang/Hoi An in particular into a “scene”. That’s how it goes in this modern age I guess. All stated, I’m happy with my experience there, but would never return. It’s no longer the Vietnam I loved. Fast forward to Mexico City, where I’m now retired and it’s Déjà Vu all over again. Yup, I’m part of the problem I guess, that’s not lost on me. It’s getting harder and harder to find a quiet, peaceful corner in the world to make my stand. Where to next?

This is bleak. I know, I know - consumerism is a problem. But reading between the lines here in this article - the average shopper is feeling an enormous amount of stress and panic about their day to day budgets.

I have been pretty broke in my life, and for the readers out there who are looking for holiday gift-giving ideas that cost very, very little, here are some gifts I have given in the past when I have been hard up - hope it can help some of you this holiday season!:

- Writing handwritten, thoughtful letters to the people you love. You can share what you love about them and how they mean so much to you. Put a nice ribbon or bow on the letter envelope and it looks great under the Christmas tree.
- Cooking your loved one's very favorite meal. Your gift can be an invite on a nice little card that shows what the menu will be. Everyone loves a home cooked meal! Get some fresh bread and butter or a salad mix for an appetizer and make the entree - boom, you have a coursed dinner!
- Develop and frame a picture of one of their favorite memories. It is cheap to develop a picture at Walgreen's/CVS/Walmart, and you can thrift a nice frame.
-  The thrift store - find a nice flannel or scarf for under $5, launder it nicely, and fold it in some gift wrap.

The thought is what matters, and with a little care into how you present something, you can have an affordable gift that means a lot. You don't have to go in debt or go to an expensive store to make the holidays fun and memorable.

This is a good piece, worth reading, and I am happy for the orchestra and its new permanent conductor, Mr. Dudamel. He has certainly not lacked for coverage and publicity in The New York Times, which is as it should be, and increasingly rare in our somewhat demented musical culture. 

But it brings up a question. Mr. Dudamel is now 45 years old. Let's say that Mr. Dudamel passes on 40 years from now at the age of 85. Will The Times obituary section then not bother to note his passing because he is no longer part of the Musical Scene as he had been 40 years earlier? 

I ask this because a Metropolitan Opera star singer who sang almost 300 performances there and retired 35 years ago died almost three weeks ago, and The Times has still not bothered to publish her obituary. She was 85 at her passing, and her name was Judith Blegen. It is unconscionable that her passing has not been covered, and I will continue to write, taking advantage of any pertinent open comment section to call attention to this situation, until that obituary appears. 

What is wrong with you people?

comments.name: Michael Rowley
comments.body:
When I was a teenager in the 70s, saying you had your ‘paraphernalia’ on you didn't mean you were carrying a bride's personal belongings aside from a dowry (it’s etymological origins); it meant you had your rolling kit, Zig-Zag papers, a bong, a pipe, roach clips, a lighter, stash boxes, and maybe some incense.

Law enforcement needed a standardized legal term to categorize this gear. They resurrected the old legal word ‘paraphernalia’ and tacked it onto anti-drug statutes (creating the phrase ‘drug paraphernalia’).

Because the term was used so heavily in courtrooms, police blotters, and evening news broadcasts, it would be comical to ask, “Anyone seen my tennis paraphernalia?” People would assume you were hitting something other than fuzzy green balls.

comments.name: Bill Batten
comments.body:
Readers who like this book should check out the hockey memoirs and films written and produced by Dave Bidini, rhythm guitarist and (mostly) backing vocalist of the Rheostatics, a Toronto based band that won multiple Juno awards (Canada's answer to the Grammys. He and his beer league team, The MorningStars, began an arts based league (1/2 your team has to work in the arts) in Toronto that has grown to include similar leagues in more than 50 cities and an Easter weekend tournament that sees 40-50 teams from across Canada competing in 4 divisions. 
Playing in that league was the most fun I've had on skates, and the networking I witnessed led to a lot of jobs for players and a few big breaks for some musicians and actor, but the best part was the joy of playing for bragging rights and, most of all, the comradery not just in your own dressing room but between teams all over the rinks and bars we frequented.
Dave captures the love of the game and the ethos that keeps us playing long after we should probably hang them up and the way hockey connects us to our 10 year old selves in a funny and intimate manner. In his books and films he explores hockey at every level from the house and rep leagues of one's youth to the grind of the NHL, and the through line is always the same: love of the game and teammates and for the magic of being turned into a kid again every time you lace 'em up.
Looking forward to Mr. Paumgarten's contribution to hockey lit, thanks for the heads up!

Turkey claims to be a global leader in climate action. But is it really? How credible is it for a country struggling with serious problems ranging from environmental policy and justice to the economy, education, press freedom, and workers' rights to present itself as a success story on the international stage?

But Turkey is not the only issue. Europe, which criticizes Turkey over democracy and environmental protection, is itself part of a system that exports its waste to other countries, putting the environment and public health at risk. If Turkey opens the door to this trade, it is complicit. But the European countries exporting their waste are equally responsible.

The same double standards apply to democracy and human rights. Western governments that put legal principles, freedom, and democratic values aside whenever their own interests are at stake are hardly in a position to claim moral superiority.

Turkey's record deserves scrutiny, but Europe's hands are far from clean. No one should dump their own garbage in someone else's backyard and then lecture them on environmental responsibility.
